questions.question_text: A description of how specific coastal features aided pirate activity.
questions.explanation: Paragraph B explains that "the numerous coves along the coast providing places for them to hide their boats and strike undetected".

questions.question_text: An instance where government officials themselves committed an act of piracy.
questions.explanation: Paragraph E describes an event in 355 BCE where Athenian ambassadors "made a detour from their official travel to capture a ship... taking the wealth found onboard for themselves".

questions.question_text: A mention of the first specific names given to pirate groups in historical records.
questions.explanation: Paragraph D mentions the "Amarna Letters" which recorded two distinct groups: "the Lukka and the Sherden".

questions.question_text: The contrast between the modern cultural image of pirates and their ancient reality.
questions.explanation: Paragraph A contrasts the modern image of Caribbean "swashbucklers" with the ancient Mediterranean pirates who operated thousands of years earlier.

questions.question_text: An explanation of how Rome turned former pirates into useful citizens.
questions.explanation: Paragraph G states that as a long-term solution, many pirates "were offered land in fertile areas... Rome got productive farmers that further boosted its economy".

question_groups.group_instruction:
Look at the following statements (Questions 27-32) and the list of researchers below. Match each statement with the correct researcher or group, A-E.
Write the correct letter, A-E, in boxes 27-32 on your answer sheet.
NB: You may use any letter more than once.
question_groups.shared_content:
List of Researchers
A. Stephan Lewandowsky & Elizabeth Marsh
B. René Descartes
C. Baruch Spinoza
D. Erik Asp & Daniel Gilbert
E. Food and Drug Administration (FDA)

questions.question_text: People initially accept all information as true before a secondary mental process evaluates it.
questions.explanation: Spinoza argued that "people accept all encountered information (or misinformation) by default and then subsequently verify or reject it through a separate cognitive process".

questions.question_text: Misinformation can cause a group of people to develop false beliefs that have negative social impacts.
questions.explanation: Lewandowsky and Marsh suggested that "misperceptions... especially when they occur among large groups of people, may have detrimental, downstream consequences for health, social harmony, and the political climate".

questions.question_text: Humans only accept or reject a piece of information after they have actively weighed its truthfulness.
questions.explanation: Descartes argued that "a person only accepts or rejects information after considering its truth or falsehood".

questions.question_text: The brain uses different physical areas for processing new information versus applying doubt to it.
questions.explanation: The research of Asp and Gilbert found that the pattern of encoding information as true is "consistent with the observation that mental resources for skepticism physically reside in a different part of the brain".

questions.question_text: Even after being corrected, false information can still continue to influence a person’s perspective.
questions.explanation: The passage notes that even with the FDA's monitoring, "even misinformation that is successfully corrected can continue to affect attitudes".

questions.question_text: Inaccurate information can lead individuals to behave differently than they would if they knew the facts.
questions.explanation: The research teams of Lewandowsky and Marsh suggested misinformation can lead people to "think and act differently than they would if they were correctly informed".
